title: CS 180 Project 4: Image Warping and Mosaicing
text:
Three pairs shot in Cupertino with the iPhone 17 Pro’s 1× camera. For each pair I kept the phone in place and only rotated it (about 17–19°), so the two photos share a center of projection and are related by a homography. The photos overlap by 64–69%.
Set 1: Visitor Center sign




Left: road and crosswalk





Right (reference): sign and olive tree at the corner



Set 2: Olive tree path




Left: path through the olive trees





Right (reference): olive trees and black louvered building



Set 3: Apartment walkway




Left: left building and walkway





Right (reference): walkway and right building






A homography maps \((x, y)\) to \((x', y')\) up to scale:
\[
\begin{bmatrix} w x' \\ w y' \\ w \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Dividing out \(w\) and clearing the denominator gives two linear equations per correspondence:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
x & y & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -x x' & -y x' \\
0 & 0 & 0 & x & y & 1 & -x y' & -y y'
\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf h
=
\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\mathbf h = (a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h)^\top.
\]
Stacking \(n\) correspondences gives a \(2n \times 8\) system \(A\mathbf h = \mathbf b\), which I solve with least squares. I clicked 15 correspondences per pair, spread across the overlap.



Set 1: numbered correspondences between the left photo and the reference





Set 2: numbered correspondences between the left photo and the reference





Set 3: numbered correspondences between the left photo and the reference


Example (Set 1). The first correspondence, \((779.17, 693.52) \to (408.11, 672.04)\), gives the first two rows of the \(30 \times 8\) system:
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
779.17 & 693.52 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 & -317987.07 & -283032.45 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & 779.17 & 693.52 & 1 & -523633.41 & -466073.18
\end{bmatrix}
\mathbf h
=
\begin{bmatrix} 408.11 \\ 672.04 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Recovered homographies (left photo → right photo):
\[
H_1 = \begin{bmatrix}
1.5195 & 0.0606 & -683.89 \\
0.2781 & 1.3733 & -267.93 \\
4.060 \times 10^{-4} & 3.359 \times 10^{-5} & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\]
\[
H_2 = \begin{bmatrix}
1.4675 & 0.0114 & -607.27 \\
0.2970 & 1.3179 & -251.65 \\
3.770 \times 10^{-4} & 1.331 \times 10^{-5} & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\]
\[
H_3 = \begin{bmatrix}
1.4589 & 0.0014 & -504.99 \\
0.2993 & 1.3310 & -271.69 \\
3.682 \times 10^{-4} & 2.845 \times 10^{-5} & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]



Inverse warping: I send the image corners through \(H\) to get the output bounding box, then map every output pixel back through \(H^{-1}\) and sample the source. Pixels that map outside the source get alpha 0.

Nearest neighbor: round to the closest pixel.
Bilinear: with \(x_0 = \lfloor x \rfloor\), \(\alpha = x - x_0\) (and \(y_0\), \(\beta\) likewise),

\[
I(x, y) = (1-\alpha)(1-\beta)\, I_{x_0, y_0} + \alpha(1-\beta)\, I_{x_0+1, y_0} + (1-\alpha)\beta\, I_{x_0, y_0+1} + \alpha\beta\, I_{x_0+1, y_0+1}.
\]


I click the four corners of a rectangular object and map them to a rectangle with its aspect ratio: 22 × 28 in for the poster frame, 8.5 × 11 in for the flyer, and about 1.6 : 1 (estimated) for the menu board.

Bilinear is about 2× slower, since it reads four pixels instead of one. Zoomed in, nearest neighbor gives jagged, blocky letter edges where the photo is enlarged, while bilinear stays smooth and only slightly softer. The quality is worth the cost, so I use bilinear for the mosaics.

Rectification 2: flyer: nearest neighbor (left) vs. bilinear (right), zoomed





Rectification 3: menu board: nearest neighbor (left) vs. bilinear (right), zoomed







Keep the right photo fixed and warp the left photo into its frame, on a canvas that fits both.
Give each image a weight that is 1 at its center and falls to 0 at its edges (a distance transform), warped along with the image.
Blend in two bands so that small misalignments don’t show up as doubled edges:

Low band (Gaussian blur, \(\sigma = 8\)): weighted average, so brightness changes fade across the overlap.
High band (image minus blur): taken from whichever image has the larger weight at each pixel.

Add the two bands to get the mosaic.
